title: Molecular CPT Codes: Tiers, 81479 and What the Code Includes
summary: Learn how molecular pathology codes moved from stacked step codes to gene-specific Tier 1 and Tier 2 codes, the classic Tier 1 examples (EGFR 81235, prothrombin 81240, JAK2 81270), when the unlisted code 81479 applies, and why slide scraping is not billable microdissection.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 67 Hits 6, 7, 8, 9 and 12 and Traps 2 and 4. Coding history and tiers from the AMP Economics 101 report (Sireci 2020) and Lynch 2018; code descriptors from the CMS Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule public-use file (CY2026 Q4, read as CSV); bundling, slide scraping, microdissection, 81479 and G0452 rules from the Medicare NCCI Policy Manual Chapter X (revision 1/1/2024; the 2025 and 2026 chapter URLs returned 404 when tried, so the 2024 revision was read). Qualifications recorded: slide scraping is included and is not microdissection (rv-ch67-scraping-not-microdissection); 81479 only when no code of any family fits, with documentation (rv-ch67-81479-scope); codes published January 2012, Medicare adoption 2013 (rv-ch67-mopath-codes-2012-2013); US-only coding (rv-ch67-cpt-us-only). Not taught: reimbursement phases (Hit 10), FDA clearance and report disclaimer (Hit 11, Trap 3).

objectives: Distinguish Tier 1 from Tier 2 molecular pathology codes and explain why gene-specific codes replaced stacked step codes.
Match the Tier 1 examples 81235, 81240, 81270 and 81201 to their defined tests, and recognize that another variant of the same gene can carry a different code.
State what a molecular pathology code already includes, why slide scraping is not microdissection, and when the unlisted code 81479 is used.

scenes.title: Three claims on one desk
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a molecular laboratory’s coder has three claims to code. (1) EGFR testing on a lung tumor block, where the technologist scraped the tumor area off an unstained slide before extraction; the draft claim adds a microdissection code. (2) A factor 2 (prothrombin) 1199G>A test, coded on the same line as the 20210G>A test because “it is the same gene”. (3) A new in-house gene test that no code names; the draft claim uses the nearest Tier 1 code. Question token: “Which code fits each test?”

cues.text: A coder has three claims. First, EGFR testing on a lung tumor, where the technologist scraped tumor off an unstained slide, and the draft adds a microdissection code.
Second, a prothrombin 1199 G to A test, coded like the 20210 test because it is the same gene. Third, a new test no code names, put under the nearest Tier 1 code.
Which code fits each test, and what does a molecular code already include?

scenes.title: From stacked steps to named analytes
scenes.altText: Timeline schematic. Old system (from 1993): one code per technical step (extraction, amplification, probe), stacked in multiples, so a payer could see that a molecular test was done but not which gene (for example, the old code 83912, discontinued in 2013). New system: analyte-specific CPT molecular pathology codes were first published in January 2012; Medicare (CMS) adopted them in 2013, paid them on the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule as technical-only codes, and created HCPCS G0452 for physician interpretation. Two tiers card: Tier 1 = commonly performed, analyte-specific codes; Tier 2 = less common analytes grouped into nine codes, 81400 to 81408, for nine levels of increasing technical complexity (level 1 example: a single germline variant; level 9 example: more than 50 exons of one gene sequenced).

cues.text: Older molecular codes described steps, not genes. Labs stacked codes for extraction, amplification and probes, so a payer could see that a molecular test was done, but not which gene.

Gene-specific codes were first published in January 2012, and Medicare adopted them in 2013. It pays them on the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule, with a separate code, G0452, for a physician’s interpretation.
Tier 1 codes name commonly performed analytes, one code per gene test or variant set.

Tier 2 groups less common analytes into nine codes, 81400 to 81408, by rising technical complexity. For example, level 1 covers single germline variants, and level 9 covers more than fifty exons of one gene.

scenes.title: One code, one defined test
scenes.altText: Tier 1 examples (descriptors paraphrased from the CMS Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule file, 2026 Q4): 81235 EGFR common variants, example non-small cell lung cancer: exon 19 LREA deletion, L858R, T790M, G719A, G719S, L861Q. 81240 F2 (prothrombin) 20210G>A variant, example hereditary hypercoagulability. 81270 JAK2 p.Val617Phe (V617F) variant, example myeloproliferative disorder. 81201 APC full gene sequence. Same-gene card: F2 1199G>A is NOT on 81240; it is listed under Tier 2 level 1, 81400, so the code follows the defined test, not just the gene name.

cues.text: Tier 1 codes describe a defined test. 81235 is EGFR common variants, the lung cancer set: exon 19 deletions, L858R, T790M, G719A, G719S and L861Q.
81240 is the prothrombin, factor 2, 20210 G to A variant, used for example in hereditary hypercoagulability. 81270 is JAK2 V617F, for myeloproliferative disorders.
And 81201 is the full gene sequence of APC. Each Tier 1 code names the gene and exactly what is analyzed.
So the same gene can fall under different codes. Prothrombin 1199 G to A is not on 81240; it is listed in Tier 2, level 1, code 81400.

scenes.title: What the code already pays for
scenes.altText: Bundle card (Medicare NCCI Policy Manual, Chapter X, section F): molecular pathology procedure codes include all aspects of sample preparation, cell lysis, internal measures to assure adequate DNA or RNA quantity (quantitation of extracted nucleic acid is included and is not billed separately, for example with spectrophotometry code 84311), and performance of the assay. Scraping tumor off an unstained slide is included and must not be reported as microdissection. Microdissection card: CPT 88380 and 88381 describe microdissection, the sample preparation of microscopically identified target cells. Unlisted card: 81479 is used only when no existing code describes the test, usually with documentation of the procedure and medical necessity; a claim is denied if an appropriate code exists. Hook answer card.

cues.text: Medicare’s coding rules say a molecular pathology code already includes sample preparation, cell lysis, checks that there is enough DNA or RNA, including quantitation, and the assay itself.

Scraping tumor off an unstained slide is part of that bundle, and must not be billed as microdissection. True microdissection, of microscopically identified target cells, has its own codes, 88380 and 88381.

When no existing code describes a test, the lab uses 81479, the unlisted molecular pathology code, usually with documentation of what was done and why. If a fitting code exists, an unlisted claim is denied.
Back to the hook. Drop the microdissection code for the scraping. Code prothrombin 1199 under 81400. And bill the new test as 81479 with documentation, not under a borrowed Tier 1 code.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Bill a novel test under the nearest Tier 1 code” (✓ codes are analyte-specific; if no code fits, use 81479 with documentation); “Scraping tumor off a slide is billable microdissection” (✓ scraping is included in the molecular code; microdissection codes 88380/88381 describe sample preparation of microscopically identified target cells); “One gene, one code” (✓ F2 20210G>A is 81240 but F2 1199G>A is 81400; JAK2 V617F is 81270).

cues.text: Trap one: bill a new test under the nearest Tier 1 code. No: codes name specific analytes. If none fits, use 81479 with documentation.
Trap two: scraping tumor off a slide is billable microdissection. No: scraping is included in the molecular code; microdissection codes are for microscopically targeted cells.
Trap three: one gene, one code. No: prothrombin 20210 is 81240, but prothrombin 1199 is 81400.

scenes.title: Name it, level it, or leave it blank
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “NAME it, LEVEL it, or leave it BLANK: a named analyte gets its Tier 1 code; a listed rarer analyte gets its Tier 2 level (1 to 9); nothing fits, the blank form, 81479. And the code buys the whole kitchen, from lysis to read-out, but true microdissection is a separate trip to the market.” Tokens: Name = Tier 1 · Level = Tier 2 · Blank = 81479. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: name it, level it, or leave it blank. A named analyte gets its Tier 1 code, a listed rarer one gets its Tier 2 level, and if nothing fits, the blank form, 81479. The code buys the whole kitchen, from lysis to read-out.
Where it breaks: there are other code families too, such as gene panel and proprietary test codes, which must be checked before 81479; codes are revised every year; and payer rules differ.

explanation.what: Plain language: a molecular billing code names exactly which gene test was done, not the lab steps used to do it. Common tests have their own named code (Tier 1); rarer ones share nine codes sorted by how hard the test is (Tier 2); a test that fits no code goes under a single unlisted code. The code already pays for preparing the sample and running the test. Scientific terms: CPT (Current Procedural Terminology), Tier 1, Tier 2 (levels 1 to 9, 81400 to 81408), unlisted molecular pathology procedure (81479), Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule, HCPCS G0452, National Correct Coding Initiative (NCCI), microdissection (88380, 88381).
explanation.why: Stacked step codes showed only that some molecular test was done, not which analyte, so payers could not tell what they were paying for; analyte-specific, method-agnostic codes fixed that. Under Medicare coding rules the preparation steps are paid within the molecular code rather than billed as extra codes; the unlisted code covers a test that no existing code describes, until a specific code is established, and a claim is denied if an appropriate code exists.
explanation.measure: Tier 1 examples: 81235 EGFR common variants (exon 19 LREA deletion, L858R, T790M, G719A, G719S, L861Q); 81240 F2 20210G>A; 81270 JAK2 V617F; 81201 APC full gene sequence. Tier 2: 81400 (level 1, for example single germline variants such as F2 1199G>A) to 81408 (level 9, for example more than 50 exons of one gene). Unlisted: 81479. Microdissection: 88380, 88381. Physician interpretation (Medicare): G0452.
explanation.differs: Tier 1 (one named analyte or variant set) vs Tier 2 (lists of rarer analytes grouped by complexity level); a specific code vs 81479 (only when none fits); slide scraping (included in the molecular code) vs microdissection of microscopically identified target cells (its own codes); technical molecular code (lab fee schedule) vs physician interpretation (G0452).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: pick 81479 for a test with no code, match a variant to its Tier 1 code (V617F 81270, 20210G>A 81240, EGFR common variants 81235), place a single germline variant in Tier 2 level 1, or decide whether a preparation step is billed separately.

questions.stem: A laboratory validates a new molecular test for a gene that no Tier 1, Tier 2, gene panel or proprietary laboratory analysis code describes. How should it be coded?

options.text: 81479, the unlisted molecular pathology code, with documentation of the procedure and its medical necessity
options.rationale: Correct. 81479 is used when no existing code describes the service, and claims usually need supporting documentation.

options.text: The Tier 1 code for the most similar gene
options.rationale: Incorrect. Tier 1 codes name specific analytes; using one for a different test misdescribes the service.

options.text: Tier 2 level 9 (81408), because the test is new
options.rationale: Incorrect. Tier 2 levels list specific analytes by complexity; being new does not place a test there.

options.text: Separate codes for extraction, amplification and detection
options.rationale: Incorrect. Stacked step codes were replaced by analyte-specific codes (adopted by Medicare in 2013), and under Medicare rules the preparation steps are included in the molecular code.

questions.stem: Which test is described by Tier 1 code 81235?

options.text: EGFR common variants, such as exon 19 deletions, L858R, T790M, G719A/S and L861Q
options.rationale: Correct. 81235 is EGFR gene analysis for common variants, typically in non-small cell lung cancer.
Incorrect. JAK2 V617F is Tier 1 code 81270.
Incorrect. APC full gene sequence is Tier 1 code 81201.

questions.stem: Before EGFR testing, a technologist scrapes the marked tumor area off an unstained slide, extracts DNA and measures its concentration. Under Medicare coding rules, what is billed for these steps?

options.text: Nothing extra: scraping, extraction and quantitation are included in the molecular pathology code
options.rationale: Correct. The NCCI manual includes sample preparation, lysis and quantitation in the molecular code, and says scraping must not be reported as microdissection.
Incorrect. Scraping tumor off an unstained slide is not microdissection; microdissection codes describe preparation of microscopically identified target cells.

options.text: A spectrophotometry code for measuring the DNA
options.rationale: Incorrect. Quantitation of extracted DNA or RNA is included and must not be billed with another code such as 84311.

options.text: The unlisted code 81479 for the extraction step
options.rationale: Incorrect. 81479 describes a whole test with no fitting code, not a preparation step of a coded test.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 67 Hit 12 and Trap 4 say pre-extraction procedures such as microdissection sit outside the Tier 1/2 bundle and are separately billable. The Medicare NCCI manual qualifies this: scraping tumor off an unstained slide is included in the molecular code and must not be reported as microdissection (88380/88381); quantitation of extracted nucleic acid is also included. The lesson teaches that distinction (register flag rv-ch67-scraping-not-microdissection).

Ch. 67 Hit 7 and Trap 2 describe 81479 as the code for any test not in Tier 1 or Tier 2. Other code families (genomic sequencing panel, multianalyte and proprietary laboratory analysis codes) must be checked first; 81479 needs documentation, and NCCI also allows component codes for a multigene test with no fitting code (register flag rv-ch67-81479-scope).

Ch. 67 Hit 6 says the codes were revised January 2013. The AMP report says the analyte-specific codes were first published in January 2012 and CMS deferred adoption until 2013; the lesson teaches both dates (register flag rv-ch67-mopath-codes-2012-2013).

CPT codes, the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule, G0452 and NCCI rules are US (Medicare) systems that change yearly. Philippine coding and reimbursement are not covered; MTLE candidates should check local rules (register flag rv-ch67-cpt-us-only).
